title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Percutaneous transluminal coronary arteriography or invasive coronary angiogram is considered the goal standard investigation tool to diagnose coronary artery disease. Coronary disease is the leading cause of death in the United States of America. The fundamental goal of a coronary angiogram is to define the coronary anatomy and determine the severity of the stenosis in epicardial coronary arteries or coronary artery bypass grafts. The heart team approach is essential for performing coronary angiograms and deciding on a revascularization strategy. Coronary angiogram through the radial approach is associated with early recovery and a low risk of access site bleeding compared to the femoral approach. A coronary angiogram is relatively safe with advanced cath lab armamentarium and technologies. However, life-threatening complications can occur occasionally. In general, revascularization can be considered if the angiographically estimated severity of coronary stenosis is more than 70%. If the stenosis is between 50-70%, it is recommended to evaluate the lesion with physiological assessment, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), or optical coherence tomography (OCT). It will guide interventional cardiologists in determining the stenosis's severity and revascularization options.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Introduction
content: Percutaneous transluminal coronary angiography (PTCA) or invasive coronary angiography is considered the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease. Coronary disease is the leading cause of death in the United States of America. Around 20.1 million adults have coronary disease in the United States. [1] More than 1 million coronary angiograms are performed annually in the USA. Dr. Sones performed the first coronary angiogram in 1958. [2] The field of Interventional Cardiology has evolved significantly since then. The fundamental goal of a coronary angiogram is to define the coronary anatomy and determine the severity of the stenosis in epicardial coronary arteries or coronary artery bypass grafts.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Introduction
content: A coronary angiogram is relatively safe and carries prognostic value. [3] However, complications like pain, bleeding, radiation-associated injury, acute kidney injury, major heart attack, stroke, blood transfusions, access site infection, and symptoms from athero-embolism, arrhythmias, and death can occur. In general, most interventional cardiologists agree that hemodynamically significant coronary disease occurs if the angiographically estimated severity of the stenosis is more than 70% (see Graph. The Effect of Coronary Artery Stenosis on Coronary Flow Reserve). If the stenosis is between 50% and 70%, it is recommended that the lesion be evaluated using physiological assessment, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), or optical coherence tomography (OCT). [4] It guides interventional cardiologists in assessing stenosis severity and selecting revascularization options.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Anatomy
content: The left main coronary artery arises from the left coronary sinus of the aorta and divides into the left anterior descending artery (LAD)and the left circumflex artery (LCx). The left anterior descending artery gives off-diagonal branches, which supply arterial blood to the anterolateral myocardium, and anterior septal branches, which supply blood to the anterior interventricular septum and anterolateral papillary muscles. The terminal part of the LAD provides the left ventricular apex. The left circumflex artery divides into obtuse marginal branches. It supplies blood to the posterolateral side of the left ventricle (see Image. Left Coronary Angiogram, Various Orthogonal Views). [5]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Anatomy
content: The right coronary artery originates from the right coronary sinus of the aorta. It travels along the right atrioventricular groove and divides into the posterolateral branch and the posterior descending artery. It also gives rise to the sinoatrial nodal artery and the right ventricular marginal artery. The posterior descending artery determines coronary circulation dominance. The right dominant circulation is widespread because, 80-85%of the time, PDA comes from the right coronary artery (see Image. Right Coronary Angiogram, Two Orthogonal Views). [5]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Anatomy
content: Anomalous coronary arteries are relatively rare (1-2%). Among them, Anomalous circumflex arteries arising from the right coronary sinus or the right coronary artery are common. It is considered a benign clinical course. Very rarely, anomalous coronary arteries traverse between the aorta and pulmonary artery, which can be associated with a malignant clinical course. [5]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Physiology
content: Epicardial coronary arteries (>400 micrometers) divide into small arteries (<400 micrometers) and eventually into arterioles (<100 micrometers), which further divide into capillaries (<10 micrometers). Coronary blood flow is greater during diastole than during systole. The epicardial coronary artery transports blood to smaller arteries. Smaller arteries and arterioles regulate coronary blood flow through autoregulation. Small arteries, Arterioles, and capillaries determine the index of microcirculatory resistance. Coronary flow reserve (CFR) depends on blood transport, autoregulation, and metabolite exchange at the capillary level (see Graph. Coronary Macro and Microcirculation). Physiological assessment of epicardial coronary stenosis measured by fractional flow reserve (FFR) and microvascular resistance measured by the index of microcirculatory resistance. Instantaneous wave-free ratio (IFR) can be used in place of fractional flow reserve. [6]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Indications
content: High-risk noninvasive testing (more than 3% annual myocardial infarction or death). Stress ischemia involves more than 10% of the myocardium or more than 2 coronary territories. Stress-induced left ventricular dysfunction (Ejection fraction less than 45% or >10% drop from the baseline). ST depressions more than 2 mm at low workload or persisting into recovery. Coronary artery calcium scores more than 400 Agaston. Stress-induced left ventricular dilatation. Inducible wall motion abnormalities in more than 2 coronary artery territories. Inducible wall motion abnormality at low-dose dobutamine or low heart rate. Left main more than 50% stenosis or multivessel disease with more than 70% stenosis. Exercise-induced ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, or ST elevations.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Contraindications -- Absolute Contraindication
content: Extremely limited life expectancy with no clinical benefit from coronary revascularization. Relative Contraindications (Applicable for non-emergent coronary angiograms) Acute on chronic kidney injury; end-stage renal disease. Active bleeding; severe anemia with unknown etiology. Severe hemorrhagic disorder. Platelets less than 50,000. Recent direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) or Coumadin use. Recent thrombotic or hemorrhagic stroke. [8] [9] Severe sepsis and septic shock; Untreated bacteremia. Altered mental status/ Unable to follow commands. Acute pulmonary edema. A patient who refused pre-treatment for contrast allergy. Status post cardiac arrest with unfavorable resuscitation features present (PH <7.2, elevated lactate >7, age more than 85, ESRD, >30 min to ROSC, no bystander CPR, unwitnessed cardiac arrest).

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Preparation -- Step 1
content: The catheterization lab charge nurse or scheduler contacts the patient to provide preoperative instructions. Nothing by mouth for 6-8 hours. Not to take anticoagulants. Discuss patient transportation options before and after the procedure. Review of home medications with a patient. Review of patient allergies. Review of the patient's labs, chest x-ray, urinalysis, and other preoperative testing. Review of the indication for a coronary angiogram with the patient. Expected time of the procedure. Expected time to check in at the catheterization lab.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Preparation -- Step 2
content: The catheterization lab nurse accompanies the patient from the check-in counter to the catheterization lab. Safely lock the patient's items. The patient wears a surgical gown. The nurse records the patient's vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and respiratory rate). Insertion of intravenous access, preferably 1 on both arms. Connect the patient to the telemetry and the blood pressure monitor. Obtain baseline EKG. Review of all the blood work and preoperative testing with the patient. Brief physical examination. Intravenous hydration should be initiated based on the patient's clinical condition (Normal saline is preferable to N-acetylcysteine or bicarbonate solutions).

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Arterial Access
content: Common femoral artery access: Under fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, obtain common femoral artery access with an 18-gauge, 25-gauge, or 25-gauge guide arch needle. Once blood flow pulsatility is confirmed, advance a 0.35 in J-wire or a 0.14 in microwire through the needle into the common femoral artery and the iliac arteries under fluoroscopic guidance. Remove the needle Introduce 5 French or 6 French access sheaths over the wire into the common femoral artery in a retrograde fashion. Connect the access sheath side port to the intravenous pressure flush line. Inject 50: 50 through the side port into the sheet and perform a femoral artery angiogram. Flush the sheath frequently

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Arterial Access
content: Radial or Ulnar artery access: Under ultrasound guidance, obtain radial /ulnar artery access with a 25-gauge microneedle. Once blood flow pulsatility is confirmed, advance the 0.14 in microwire through the needle into the radial/ulnar artery, and remove the needle. Introducing a 5 French or 6 French access sheath over the wire into the radial/ulnar artery in a retrograde fashion. Connect the access sheath side port to the intravenous pressure flush line. Inject radial cocktail (nitroglycerin, nicardipine, or verapamil) and intravenous heparin through the side port. Flush the sheath frequently.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Left main coronary artery cannulation:
content: Advance diagnostic catheters (JL, AL, Jacky, or Tiger) over the wire under fluoroscopy guidance. Once a catheter tip is in the left coronary sinus, remove the 0.35 in support wire. Obtain aortic pressure and waveform for baseline measurements. Engage the left main coronary artery with a slow, steady clock, counter-clock, and push-and-pull maneuver. The left anterior oblique view is preferred to engage the left main coronary artery. Obtain angiogram pictures by injecting intravenous contrast into the left main with steady pressure. It is crucial to review pressure tracing and an EKG before the injection. Avoid injecting contrast if pressure is dampened. Obtain angiographic images in the right anterior oblique caudal, right anterior oblique cranial, left anterior oblique cranial, and left anterior oblique caudal projections. Exchange the catheter over the wire under fluoroscopic guidance. (Media Item 2)

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Saphenous venous bypass graft (SVG) cannulation:
content: Advance diagnostic catheters over the wire under fluoroscopy guidance. Preferably, JR, AR, and AL catheters are for SVG to left-sided grafts, and multipurpose catheters for SVG to RCA grafts. Once a catheter tip is in the SVG ostium or near the radiopaque marker, remove the 0.35 in support wire. Obtain aortic pressure and waveform for baseline measurements. Engage SVG with slow and steady clock, counter clock, and push and pull movements. The right anterior oblique view is preferred to engage left-sided SVG grafts, and the Left anterior oblique is preferred to engage right-sided grafts. Obtain angiogram pictures by injecting intravenous contrast into the SVG with steady pressure. It is crucial to review pressure tracing an EKG before the injection. Avoid injecting contrast if the pressure is dampened. Obtain angiographic images in the right anterior oblique, left anterior oblique, and left anterior oblique cranial or caudal views. Exchange the catheter over the wire under fluoroscopic guidance.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Internal mammary artery (IMA) cannulation:
content: Advance diagnostic catheters (AR or IMA catheters) over the wire under fluoroscopy guidance. Once a catheter tip is in the IMA ostium, remove 0.35 in support wire. Obtain aortic pressure and waveform for baseline measurements. Engage IMA with slow, steady clock, counter-clock, and push-and-pull movements. Anteroposterior or Right anterior oblique view is preferred to engage LIMA, and left anterior oblique is preferred to engage RIMA. Obtain angiogram pictures by injecting intravenous contrast into the IMA with steady pressure. It is essential to review pressure tracing an EKG before the injection. Avoid injecting contrast if the pressure is dampened. Obtain angiogram pictures in right anterior oblique cranial and left anterior oblique cranial views. Exchange the catheter over the wire under fluoroscopic guidance. Left radial access is preferred if the left internal mammary artery is present. Before engaging the internal mammary artery, one should engage the subclavian artery in the femoral access approach.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Technique or Treatment -- Post-angiogram steps:
content: Review the angiogram pictures once they are completed. Remove catheters over the wire under fluoroscopic guidance. Consider a closure device if the access site is optimal at the common femoral artery. Apply the transradial band for the radial or ulnar access site. Transfer the patient to the post-procedure recovery area. Monitor blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and rhythm changes closely. Once the patient has recovered from sedation and vital signs are within normal limits, consider discharge if inpatient care is unnecessary. Discussed the angiogram results with the patient and family in detail. Arrange outpatient follow-up. Review the medications before discharge.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Complications -- Early Complications
content: Access site hematoma. Acute Kidney Injury. Stroke (Embolic or Hemorrhagic). Thromboembolic events. Acute blood anemia requiring blood transfusion. Access site pain. Myocardial infarction (Abrupt closure of a coronary artery). Acute pulmonary edema. Emergency Coronary artery bypass surgery. VT/Vfib. Atheroemboli. Radiation-related injuries. [8] [9] A-V fistula. Pseudoaneurysm. Death

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Clinical Significance
content: A coronary angiogram delineates coronary anatomy and quantifies the severity of coronary artery stenosis. It would help interventional/invasive cardiologists plan an appropriate revascularization strategy, if indicated. Tools and techniques for coronary angiography have evolved substantially over the last 2 decades, and complication rates have decreased accordingly. A coronary angiogram is relatively safe and can be performed in a daycare setting. However, it is not entirely free of complications.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A coronary angiogram is a minimally invasive procedure and can be associated with severe complications. The heart team approach is essential to perform coronary angiograms effectively with minimal complications. The heart team approach comprises an interventional/invasive cardiologist, a general cardiologist, a catheterization lab nurse, a catheterization lab technician, a cardiothoracic surgeon, a primary care physician, or a referral physician. Closed-loop communication among the heart team can minimize complications. Meticulous patient selection is essential for coronary angiograms in stable angina patients. Always review the patient's allergies, home medications, renal function tests, hemoglobin and hematocrit, platelet count, and PT/INR before the procedure to minimize common complications. Intravenous hydration prevents contrast-induced nephropathy. It is vital to watch for pressure tracing and rhythm strips before injecting contrast into the coronary artery ostium. Effective team communication is a key factor in improved catheterization laboratory procedural outcomes. [8]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Arteriography -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: The catheterization lab nurse or Allied health care professional accompanies the patient from the check-in counter to the catheterization lab. Safely lock the patient's items. Assist the patient in donning a surgical gown. Insertion of intravenous access, preferably 1 on both arms. Connect the patient to the telemetry and the blood pressure monitor. Obtain Baseline EKG. Review of all the blood work and preoperative testing with the patient. Brief physical examination. Intravenous hydration based on the patient's clinical condition (Normal saline is preferable to N acetylcysteine and bicarbonate solution). Coordinate care and update it to the patient and the patient's family. Administering medications during the procedure.

content: Before the procedure, the nurse obtains and monitors the patient's vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and respiratory rate). Report any proceduralist if there is pressure waveform dampening, blood pressure changes, or EKG rhythm changes.
